extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of television and comedy, researchers looking up the Taskmaster TV series
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the format, task-design principles, scoring rules, filming practices, and special-episode procedures used in the British comedy panel show Taskmaster. Useful for understanding how tasks are constructed, evaluated, and produced for the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring based on performance, interpretation or other arbitrary, comedic factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Taskmaster reviews the contestants' attempts and awards points based on performance, interpretation or other arbitrary, comedic factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring is subjective and comedic rather than strictly objective; the Taskmaster (Greg Davies) exercises judgement to award points that serve the show's humour and narrative rather than only formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking 1–5 points per task
rubrics_metrics.description: Davies then judges each contestant's performance in each task to determine how many points they receive, generally ranking them from one to five points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points per task are ordinal (typically 1–5); episode winners are determined by highest score in that episode and series winners by cumulative score across episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification for failing objective, breaking rules, or cheating
rubrics_metrics.description: Contestants can be disqualified and awarded no points for a task if they fail to achieve the task's objective, inadvertently break one of the task's rules, or cheat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains a boundary between comedic creativity and actions that violate explicit task instructions or fairness; disqualification removes scoring for that task entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonus points at Taskmaster's discretion or per task instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contestants can be given bonus points, either at Davies's discretion or based on criteria described in a task's instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bonus points are a flexible scoring mechanic used to reward particularly funny, creative, or rule-abiding behaviour; some tasks explicitly define bonus criteria, others rely on the presenter's whim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-task scoring: equal score for all team members
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, contestants conduct tasks as a team with one or two other contestants; in most such cases, all members of a team receive the same score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team-based tasks remove individual differentiation for that task and treat team performance as a single judged outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasks must be read aloud from sealed instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks are typically given to the contestants by Horne who hands them a tri-folded page sealed with red wax and the 'TM' branding. The contestants must read the task out loud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalised presentation of the task emphasises ceremony and clarity; reading aloud makes the instructions part of the studio action and ensures everyone (and the audience) hears the exact brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasks designed to avoid specialist equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Horne designs the tasks to avoid the need for any specialist equipment, so that 'people at home [are] able to do the same things'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical design constraint: tasks should be reproducible by the public with ordinary household items, supporting audience engagement (HomeTasking) and reducing production complexity/cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present a single 'right way' to complete tasks (avoid prescribing correct method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initially they planned to have Horne show the right way to complete the task after showing the contestants' attempts, but this plan was abandoned as 'it supposed there was a right way'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping multiple valid approaches encourages creativity and comedic variation; the show avoids privileging a single correct solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid involving the general public in tasks where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Some tasks in the first series involved the general public, but later series avoided this in order to prevent coming across as a 'prank show'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer/creative preference to keep tone inoffensive and focused on contestant creativity rather than surprising or inconveniencing members of the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producers may veto tasks for pragmatic or safety reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Some tasks are vetoed by producers for pragmatic reasons, such as 'paint the biggest thing red'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production oversight filters out tasks that are impractical, unsafe, or likely to cause logistical or legal problems; examples show vetoed ideas and tasks that always go wrong (e.g., bubble-wrap bursting attempts not shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasks can be multi-stage or include mini-tasks; tests lateral thinking, creativity, and logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks given to contestants range from simple physical challenges to more complex or artistic tasks; some tasks may consist of multiple stages or mini-tasks. To complete tasks, contestants often have to apply a level of logic, creativity, or lateral thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Task variety is deliberate: physical, artistic, timed, staged, or multi-part tasks invite different comedic responses and show the contestants' range of problem-solving approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize task: contestants supply themed objects as episode prizes
rubrics_metrics.description: An introductory Prize task, in which each contestant supplies an object they possess that conforms to a set theme, all of which will be awarded to the winner of the episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize task doubles as a task and as the episode's trophy mechanism; themes constrain the supplied items and create additional humour/competition around prize selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live (studio) task performed onstage as part of studio segments
rubrics_metrics.description: A final 'Live' task, which the contestants perform onstage in the studio, is usually conducted during studio segments along with the Prize task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live tasks provide immediate, performative moments for studio audience reaction and can act as quick tie-breakers or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiebreaker procedure: pre-recorded or quick live task
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event of a tie in the top score at the end of the episode or series, either a pre-recorded tiebreaker task between the tied contestants is shown, or a quick live task is performed to determine the winner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible tiebreaking maintains pacing: a pre-recorded head-to-head or an on-the-night live task resolves ties without undermining episode structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filming schedule and separation to protect studio reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks are mostly pre-recorded months in advance and then screened in-studio with the contestants and presenters present. Before the studio filming, contestants are forbidden to discuss their tasks and are not shown any footage from the tasks, so that studio reactions are genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staggered production (pre-record house tasks, then studio screening) preserves spontaneity of studio commentary and ensures real-time comedic reactions; non-disclosure about tasks is enforced to protect that spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filming operational details: one day per contestant per episode; about eight tasks a day
rubrics_metrics.description: Filming tasks takes roughly one day per contestant per episode, filming around eight tasks a day, with the days of filming spread out across several months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production planning guidance: intensive single-contestant shoots maximise efficiency while spreading filming reduces scheduling conflicts; design and planning must accommodate this pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contestant composition and series structure: five contestants, mainly comedians; episode/series winners and trophies
rubrics_metrics.description: In each series a group of five celebrities (mainly comedians) attempt to complete a series of challenges. A winner is determined in each episode and for the series overall. The series' cumulative winner receives a trophy (golden bust of Davies in the main series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format requirement for casting and series scoring: consistent small group across a series supports character-driven comedy; the trophy and episodic winners create stakes and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional prank tasks and one-contestant-only tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally, prank tasks are given to one contestant alone, who is led to believe the others are performing the same task; Davies may award bonus points for these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prank or single-target tasks are used sparingly for comedic payoff; scoring discretion can be used to reward resilience, reaction, or the comedic situation produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series themes influence set, prop and musical design
rubrics_metrics.description: Each series is assigned a theme that influences the design of the house and the music that plays during tasks. Themes have included Japanese, western, art deco, Victorian, and steampunk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thematic through-line shapes visual and auditory design choices across a series, reinforcing branding and giving production designers constraints/inspiration for task props and set decoration.
